steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on a truly joint neural architecture for morphological segmentation and dependency parsing in morphologically rich languages. Cover why parsing still matters, the problem with segment-then-parse pipelines, the joint hypothesis and prior joint parsers, our lattice-based arc-factored approach, and our Hebrew results.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. Dependency parsing and why it still matters
2. Pipeline architectures and error propagation in MRLs
3. The joint hypothesis and previous joint systems
4. Neural multilingual parsers still segment-then-parse
5. Our approach: joint lattice-based arc-factored parser
6. Results on Hebrew UD

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. Dependency parsing
- task: analyze syntactic structure of a sentence, expose functional relations between words
- useful for machine translation, question answering, information extraction
- English NLP now often end-to-end with LLMs, no symbolic structure
- low- and medium-resource languages: parsers still indispensable for downstream applications

2. Pipelines and MRLs
- neural SOTA parsers presuppose pipeline: tokenization, word segmentation, POS tagging, morphological feature tagging, dependency parsing, sometimes NER
- features from each stage fed to later tasks
- MRLs: space-delimited tokens consist of multiple units, each with distinct syntactic role
- -> segmentation essential for MRL parsing
- high morphological ambiguity: segmentation before/independent of parsing -> errors propagate -> incorrect parse

3. Joint hypothesis and earlier joint systems
- joint hypothesis, heavily populated in pre-neural MRL parsing studies: segmentation and syntax mutually dependent -> solve together
- joint morpho-syntactic transition-based parser, SOTA on Hebrew; morphological lattice input, syntactic + morphological transitions, arcs and segments in tandem
- graph-based: all potential segments of any token, MST parser picks highest-scoring arcs and nodes; improvements for Hebrew and Turkish
- Sanskrit: non-neural graph-based parser, energy-based modeling, optimal path = segmentation + syntax; but non-neural, Sanskrit specific, hand-crafted features
- neural, Sanskrit: pre-training, combining word representations from encoders on auxiliary tasks (morphological, syntactic tags); no segmentation decisions, no lattice

4. Neural multilingual parsers
- segment-then-parse pipeline fully maintained
- no language-agnostic architecture for joint segmentation and parsing yet

5. Our approach
- revisit joint hypothesis for neural dependency parsing in MRLs
- start from arc-factored model: sequence of words -> highest-scoring arcs -> dependency tree
- input: linearized lattice of all possible morphological segments as potential nodes; learn head + label per node
- training: incorrect segments mapped to auxiliary node, subtree excluded from final tree
- inference: relevant segments -> main branch, unused -> auxiliary branch; complete tree
- segmentation informed by syntactic arcs and vice versa
- MTL component predicts node features, e.g. POS, gender, number, person

6. Results
- Hebrew Section of UD
- complete morphological analyses: new SOTA for segmentation and parsing, single jointly trained model
- realistic case, lattices missing analyses (OOV tokens): competitive segmentation, tagging, parsing; beats Stanza and Trankit pipelines

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Dependency parsing is the task of automatically analyzing the syntactic structure of a sentence and showing the functional relationships between its words. In the past dependency parsing was shown to be very useful for many language processing tasks, for example machine translation, question answering and information extraction. Nowadays many English NLP tasks are solved end-to-end using large language models (LLMs) without accessing any symbolic structure, but for low- and medium-resource languages parsers are still indispensable, and they enable a lot of downstream applications.

Most neural state-of-the-art dependency parsers to date assume a pipeline architecture with several analysis stages, which are tokenization, word segmentation, part-of-speech (POS) tagging, morphological feature tagging, dependency parsing, and sometimes also named entity recognition, and the linguistic features from each stage are given as input to the tasks after it and contribute to the overall efficacy. In morphologically-rich languages (MRLs), many raw space-delimited tokens consist of multiple units, and each of them has a distinct role in the overall syntactic representation. So segmentation is essential for accurate MRL parsing. But because of the high morphological ambiguity, when segmentation is done before (and independently of) the parsing phase, segmentation errors can propagate and undermine the syntactic predictions, which then leads to an overall incorrect parse.

There is the joint hypothesis, which was very common in parsing studies for MRLs in the pre-neural era. It says that morphological segmentation and syntactic predictions are mutually dependent, so these two tasks should be solved together.

Along these lines, one study developed a joint morpho-syntactic transition-based parser that got state-of-the-art (SOTA) results on Hebrew parsing. This system uses a morphological lattice as input to a transition system that has both syntactic and morphological transitions, so it picks the right arcs and segments in tandem. Another influential work displays all the potential segments that could be involved in the analysis of any token, and lets an MST graph-based parser pick the highest scoring subset of arcs and nodes as the output dependency tree, and it showed parsing improvements for both Hebrew and Turkish. In a similar way, a non-neural graph-based parser was contributed for Sanskrit, which uses energy-based modeling to find the optimal path on a graph that jointly represents a valid segmentation and syntactic analysis. But this architecture is non-neural and specific to Sanskrit, and it relies on hand-crafted feature engineering that is labor-intensive. In neural settings, and again for Sanskrit, a pre-training approach was introduced that focuses on amalgamating word representations generated by encoders trained on auxiliary tasks, such as morphological and syntactic tags. Unlike our work, this neural architecture does not make any segmentation decisions and it does not use the lattice structure for joint segmentation and parsing.

[Neural multilingual parsers]
- segment-then-parse pipeline fully maintained
- no language-agnostic architecture for joint segmentation and parsing yet

[Our approach]
- revisit joint hypothesis for neural dependency parsing in MRLs
- start from arc-factored model: sequence of words -> highest-scoring arcs -> dependency tree
- input: linearized lattice of all possible morphological segments as potential nodes; learn head + label per node
- training: incorrect segments mapped to auxiliary node, subtree excluded from final tree
- inference: relevant segments -> main branch, unused -> auxiliary branch; complete tree
- segmentation informed by syntactic arcs and vice versa
- MTL component predicts node features, e.g. POS, gender, number, person

[Results]
- Hebrew Section of UD
- complete morphological analyses: new SOTA for segmentation and parsing, single jointly trained model
- realistic case, lattices missing analyses (OOV tokens): competitive segmentation, tagging, parsing; beats Stanza and Trankit pipelines

steps.text:

But because of the high morphological ambiguity, when segmentation is done before (and independently of) the parsing phase, segmentation errors can propagate and undermine the syntactic predictions, which then leads to an overall incorrect parse.

There is the joint hypothesis, which was very common in parsing studies for MRLs in the pre-neural era. It says that morphological segmentation and syntactic predictions are mutually dependent, so these two tasks should be solved together.

Along these lines, one study developed a joint morpho-syntactic transition-based parser that got state-of-the-art (SOTA) results on Hebrew parsing. This system uses a morphological lattice as input to a transition system that has both syntactic and morphological transitions, so it picks the right arcs and segments in tandem. Another influential work displays all the potential segments that could be involved in the analysis of any token, and lets an MST graph-based parser pick the highest scoring subset of arcs and nodes as the output dependency tree, and it showed parsing improvements for both Hebrew and Turkish. In a similar way, a non-neural graph-based parser was contributed for Sanskrit, which uses energy-based modeling to find the optimal path on a graph that jointly represents a valid segmentation and syntactic analysis. But this architecture is non-neural and specific to Sanskrit, and it relies on hand-crafted feature engineering that is labor-intensive. In neural settings, and again for Sanskrit, a pre-training approach was introduced that focuses on amalgamating word representations generated by encoders trained on auxiliary tasks, such as morphological and syntactic tags. Unlike our work, this neural architecture does not make any segmentation decisions and it does not use the lattice structure for joint segmentation and parsing.

Overall, for neural multilingual dependency parsers the segment-then-parse pipeline approach is fully maintained, and a language-agnostic architecture for morphological segmentation and syntactic parsing has not been found yet.

In this paper we revisit the joint hypothesis as a viable way to improve neural dependency parsing for MRLs. The idea in short is as follows. We start with an arc-factored model that takes a sequence of words as input and generates a dependency tree by picking the highest scoring arcs that connect all the words. In our approach, the arc-factored model takes as input a linearized lattice that contains all the possible morphological segments that could act as nodes, and it learns to assign a head and a label to each of these nodes. In training, incorrect segments are mapped to an auxiliary node, and its subtree is excluded from the final dependency tree. Then at inference time the model maps the relevant segments to the main branch and the unused segments to the auxiliary branch, and builds a complete dependency tree. In this process the morphological segmentation decisions are informed by the syntactic arcs, and the other way around. We also extend the architecture with a multi-task learning (MTL) component that predicts the features of each node, e.g., POS, gender, number and person.

We run experiments on the Hebrew Section of UD. They show that when the input morphological analyses are complete, our model gives new and improved state of the art results for segmentation and parsing for Hebrew, in a single model that is jointly trained. In the more realistic case where some of the word lattices may be missing possible analyses (the case of out of vocabulary (OOV) tokens), the model still gives competitive results for segmentation, tagging and parsing, and it outperforms the state-of-the-art results of the de-facto standard pipelines, Stanza and Trankit.

In morphologically-rich languages (MRLs), many raw space-delimited tokens consist of multiple units, each serving a distinct role in the overall syntactic representation [7,8]. Segmentation is therefore essential for accurate MRL parsing. However, due to high morphological ambiguity, when segmentation is performed prior to (and independently of) parsing, segmentation errors may propagate and undermine the syntactic predictions, leading to an overall incorrect parse.

According to the joint hypothesis, which was heavily explored in parsing studies for MRLs in the pre-neural era [9,10,11,12,13], morphological segmentation and syntactic predictions are mutually dependent, and these two tasks should hence be solved together.
